11.01.title: What is a fluid
11.01.html:
Push a block of rubber sideways and it deforms a little, then stops: it resists shear with a stress that depends on how far you’ve pushed. Push the surface of the Limmat and the water keeps moving as long as you push. A fluid is a material that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small. What it resists isn’t the amount of deformation but its rate, and the property measuring that resistance is viscosity.

The continuum

Water is made of molecules, but a cubic micrometre still holds about 3×1010 of them. So we treat velocity, pressure and density as smooth fields u(x,t), p(x,t), ρ(x,t). That’s the continuum hypothesis. It fails only when the flow’s length scale approaches the mean free path, as in rarefied gas at high altitude or nanochannels.

Newton’s law of viscosity

Put fluid between two parallel plates a gap h apart, fix the bottom one and slide the top one at speed U. The fluid sticks to both walls (the no-slip condition), and the shear stress needed is

τ=μdydu​.

μ is the dynamic viscosity in Pa s: about 1.0×10−3 for water at 20 °C, 1.8×10−5 for air, 0.29 for SAE 30 oil and around 10 for honey. The kinematic viscosity ν=μ/ρ, in m²/s, appears whenever inertia competes with friction. Fluids obeying this linear law are Newtonian. Ketchup, paint, blood and toothpaste aren’t.

Couette flow

With no pressure gradient, the momentum balance on a thin slab of fluid reduces to μd2u/dy2=0, so the velocity is linear:

u(y)=Uhy​,τ=μhU​ everywhere.

Add a pressure gradient and the equation becomes μu′′=dp/dx, which adds a parabola. This is the basis of lubrication: a thin oil film in a bearing carries the load while shearing at enormous rates.

Worked exampleShearing a thin film

Top plate at 2 m/s, gap 1 mm, plate area 0.5 m².

  1. Water: τ=10−3⋅2/0.001=2.0 Pa, a force of 1.0 N.
  2. SAE 30 oil: 580 Pa, 290 N. Honey: 20 000 Pa, 10 kN.
  3. The finite-difference solution of μu′′=0 is linear to machine precision, with a constant shear rate of 2000 s⁻¹.
  4. With dp/dx=−2 MPa/m in the oil, the centre speed rises from 1.0 to 1.8621 m/s. The flow rate per metre width goes from 1.0000 to 1.5745 L/s (exact: 1.5747).

Exercise 1A journal bearing

A 50 mm shaft turns at 3000 rpm in a 40 mm long bearing with a radial clearance of 0.05 mm, filled with oil of μ=0.03 Pa s. Treating the thin film as Couette flow, find the friction torque and the power lost.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Surface speed U=πDn/60=π⋅0.05⋅3000/60=7.854 m/s.
  2. Shear stress τ=0.03⋅7.854/(5×10−5)=4712 Pa.
  3. Wetted area πDL=6.283×10−3 m², so the friction force is 29.61 N.
  4. Torque 29.61⋅0.025=0.740 N m; power Tω=0.740⋅314.16=232.5 W, which ends up as heat in the oil. This is Petroff’s equation.

11.02.title: Fluid statics
11.02.html:
Dive to the bottom of a pool and your ears hurt; drive up to the Jungfraujoch and a sealed crisp packet puffs up. Both come from one equation. In a fluid at rest there’s no shear stress, only pressure, and the pressure at a point is the same in every direction. It changes with height because each layer has to hold up the weight of everything above it.

The hydrostatic equation

Balance the forces on a small fluid element of height dz: the pressure difference across it carries its weight, so

dzdp​=−ρg.

For a liquid, ρ is constant and p=p0​+ρgh at depth h below a free surface at p0​. Ten metres of water adds 1000⋅9.81⋅10=98.1 kPa, about one atmosphere. Engineers often quote gauge pressure, measured relative to the local atmosphere, rather than absolute pressure.

For a gas, density depends on pressure: ρ=p/(RT). With the standard atmosphere’s temperature falling 6.5 K per km, integration gives p=p0​(T/T0​)g/(Rλ). Pressure falls by about 12 % per kilometre near the ground.

Manometers

A U-tube holding a dense liquid measures a pressure difference by the height difference h it supports. Walking down one leg and up the other, adding ρgΔz going down and subtracting going up,

p1​−p2​=(ρm​−ρf​)gh,

where ρm​ is the manometer fluid and ρf​ the fluid in the pipe above it. Mercury gives compact readings for large differences; water or oil gives sensitivity for small ones.

Worked exampleWater, air and mercury

  1. Gauge pressure at 10 m depth: 98.10 kPa, from integrating dp/dz=−ρg numerically.
  2. Standard atmosphere, integrated with the 6.5 K/km lapse rate: 965.2 hPa in Zurich (408 m) and 661.4 hPa on the Jungfraujoch (3454 m). The numerical integration matches the closed form to within 1 Pa.
  3. At 661.4 hPa water boils at 88.5 °C (Antoine equation), so pasta cooks slowly up there.
  4. A mercury manometer under water reading 120 mm: (13546−998)⋅9.81⋅0.120=14.772 kPa.

Exercise 1The bottom of Lake Zurich

Lake Zurich is 136 m deep at its deepest. Find the gauge and absolute pressure there, taking 96.52 kPa for atmospheric pressure at the lake surface. Then find the pressure difference read by a water manometer showing 50 mm across a fan duct carrying air (ρ=1.2 kg/m³).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Gauge: 1000⋅9.81⋅136=1.334 MPa, about 13 atmospheres.
  2. Absolute: 1.334+0.0965=1.431 MPa.
  3. Manometer: (998−1.2)⋅9.81⋅0.050=488.9 Pa. Air’s density barely matters here.

Δp (kPa) for a 200 mm mercury reading under water (ρ_m 13 546, ρ_f 998). 3 decimals.

11.03.title: Buoyancy and stability
11.03.html:
A coconut that falls into a Bali river floats away, sometimes across oceans; that’s how coconut palms spread around the tropics. A ship loaded with containers stays upright in waves, until someone stacks them too high. Both are hydrostatics. Floating is about the size of the buoyant force; staying upright is about where it acts.

Archimedes

The pressure on a submerged body is higher underneath than on top. Adding it up over the surface gives an upward force equal to the weight of displaced fluid:

FB​=ρf​gVsub​.

It acts at the centre of buoyancy B, the centroid of the displaced volume. A floating body sinks until FB​ equals its weight, so the submerged fraction is ρbody​/ρf​. A husked coconut of 1.2 kg and 1.9 litres floats 63 % submerged in fresh water.

Stability and the metacentre

Heel a floating hull by a small angle θ. Its weight still acts at the centre of gravity G, but the underwater shape changes: one side goes deeper, the other rises, and B moves towards the low side. The vertical through the new B crosses the centreline at the metacentre M. If M is above G, weight and buoyancy form a couple that pushes the hull back upright.

The height of M above B is

BM=VIwp​​,

where Iwp​ is the second moment of area of the waterplane about the roll axis and V is the displaced volume. For a box barge of beam B and draft T, BM=B2/(12T). The metacentric height is

GM=KB+BM−KG,

measured from the keel K. The hull is stable if and only if GM>0, and for small heel the righting arm is GZ≈GMsinθ. Wide hulls are stable; high loads aren’t.

Worked exampleA box barge

A barge 20 m long, 6 m beam and 2.5 m deep displaces 150 t in seawater (ρ=1025 kg/m³), with KG=1.8 m.

  1. Draft T=150000/(1025⋅20⋅6)=1.2195 m; KB=0.6098 m; BM=36/(12⋅1.2195)=2.4600 m.
  2. GM=0.6098+2.4600−1.8=1.2698 m: stable.
  3. The code finds GZ by clipping the hull polygon at a tilted waterline that keeps the displaced area constant. At 1° GZ = 0.0222 m, exactly GMsinθ; at 10° it’s 0.2271 m against 0.2205, matching the wall-sided formula GZ=sinθ(GM+21​BMtan2θ).
  4. Raising KG to 1.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 4.0 m gives GM of +2.070, +1.070, +0.070 and −0.930 m. The last one capsizes, and the sign of GZ always matches the sign of GM.

Exercise 1Deck cargo

The barge above must keep GM≥0.5 m for safety. What’s the highest allowed centre of gravity, at the same displacement?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. KGmax​=KB+BM−0.5=0.6098+2.4600−0.5=2.5698 m.
  2. The deck is 2.5 m above the keel, so the combined centre of gravity of barge and cargo may sit only about 7 cm above deck level. Heavy deck cargo must be balanced by low ballast.

11.04.title: Flow kinematics
11.04.html:
Before asking what forces drive a flow, we need ways to describe the motion itself. Drop a coconut into the Limmat and follow it, or stand on a bridge and watch the water passing one spot. Those are the two viewpoints of fluid mechanics. Then there are three different “lines” you can draw through a flow, and they only agree when nothing changes in time.

Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions

  • Lagrangian: follow individual fluid particles, xp​(t). Natural for a coconut, a drifting buoy or a smoke particle.
  • Eulerian: describe the velocity at every fixed point, u(x,t). Natural for measurements at a bridge pier, and what almost all fluid equations use.

The link is dxp​/dt=u(xp​,t): integrating the Eulerian field gives particle paths.

Three kinds of line

  • A streamline is everywhere tangent to the velocity at one instant: dx/ds∥u(x,t0​) with time frozen.
  • A pathline is the trajectory of one particle over time.
  • A streakline joins all particles that passed through one fixed point, like dye from a nozzle or smoke from a chimney.

In steady flow the field doesn’t change, so a particle simply runs along its streamline and all three coincide. In unsteady flow they differ, sometimes dramatically. A smoke trail in gusty wind is a streakline, and it doesn’t show you where the air is going now.

A worked field

Take u=U0​, v=V0​sinωt: uniform in space, but the cross-flow oscillates. At any instant the streamlines are straight parallel lines with slope V0​sin(ωt)/U0​. A particle released at the origin at t=0 follows x=U0​t, y=V0​(1−cosωt)/ω, a wave entirely above the axis. The streakline at t=2π/ω is the mirror image, entirely below.

Worked exampleTracing with RK4

U0​=1 m/s, V0​=0.5 m/s, ω=1 rad/s.

  1. Pathline from the origin over one period: it ends at (6.2832, 0) and peaks at y=1.0000=2V0​/ω, as the exact solution says.
  2. Streamline at t=π/2: straight with slope 0.5000 =V0​/U0​.
  3. Streakline at t=2π: y from −1.0000 to 0, the mirror image of the pathline.
  4. For a steady field u=1, v=0.3, all three lines lie on y=0.3x to machine precision.

Exercise 1One more particle

In the same field, where is a particle released from the origin at t0​=π when t=2π? Is that point on the pathline of the particle released at t=0, on the streakline at t=2π, or both?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. x=U0​(t−t0​)=π=3.1416 m.
  2. y=V0​(cosωt0​−cosωt)/ω=0.5(cosπ−cos2π)=−1.0 m.
  3. It’s on the streakline at 2π (all particles from the origin, by definition), at its lowest point. The pathline from t=0 at x=π is at y=+1.0, so the point isn’t on that pathline.

11.05.title: The material derivative
11.05.html:
Water flowing steadily through a nozzle speeds up as the nozzle narrows. At every fixed point nothing changes in time, yet each parcel of water accelerates, and Newton’s second law is about parcels. The material derivative is the bridge: the rate of change seen by someone riding with the fluid, written in Eulerian variables.

Following a parcel

Let q(x,t) be any field: temperature, a velocity component, a dye concentration. A parcel at xp​(t) sees q(xp​(t),t), and by the chain rule

DtDq​=∂t∂q​+u∂x∂q​+v∂y∂q​+w∂z∂q​=∂t∂q​+(u⋅∇)q.

The first term is the local change at a fixed point; the second is the convective change from moving to a place where q is different. Applied to velocity it gives the acceleration of a fluid particle:

a=DtDu​=∂t∂u​+(u⋅∇)u.

The convective term is nonlinear in u. That’s the source of most of the difficulty, and the richness, of fluid mechanics, turbulence included.

Two examples

  • Stagnation-point flow u=ax, v=−ay, like water hitting a wall: steady, yet a=(a2x,a2y). Parcels accelerate away from the wall along it and decelerate as they approach.
  • Solid-body rotation u=−Ωy, v=Ωx: steady, and a=−Ω2(x,y), the centripetal acceleration of circular motion.

Worked exampleA strengthening stagnation flow

u=a(t)x, v=−a(t)y with a=0.5(1+0.2t) s⁻¹, at (2, 1) m and t=3 s.

  1. Local acceleration (central differences in time): (0.2, −0.1) m/s².
  2. Convective: (1.28, 0.64) m/s². Total (1.48, 0.54), matching the exact (a˙x+a2x, −a˙y+a2y).
  3. Following the exact particle path and differentiating its velocity gives the same (1.48, 0.54).
  4. With a constant at 0.5, the local part vanishes but the convective acceleration at (2, 1) is still (0.5, 0.25) m/s².

Exercise 1A nozzle

In a nozzle the centreline speed is u=U0​(1+x/L) with U0​=2 m/s and L=0.5 m. Find the acceleration of a water parcel at x=0.25 m. Then let the supply ramp up so that U0​=2+t (m/s, t in s) and find it again at t=0.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. u=2(1+0.5)=3 m/s and ∂u/∂x=U0​/L=4 s⁻¹.
  2. Steady: a=u∂u/∂x=3⋅4=12 m/s², over a g, with nothing changing in time.
  3. Ramping: the local term is U˙0​(1+x/L)=1⋅1.5=1.5 m/s², so a=13.5 m/s².

11.06.title: Conservation of mass
11.06.html:
Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster. No water is created or destroyed, so what goes in must come out: squeeze the area and the speed goes up. That’s continuity, the first of the conservation laws, written once for a control volume and once for every point of the flow.

The Reynolds transport theorem

Physical laws are written for a fixed lump of matter (a system). Engineers prefer a fixed region of space, a control volume (CV), that fluid flows through. The Reynolds transport theorem links them: for any extensive property B with intensity β=B/m,

dtdBsys​​=dtd​∫CV​ρβdV+∮CS​ρβ(u⋅n)dA.

Rate of change of the system = accumulation inside + net outflow through the surface. With B = mass, β=1 and the left side is zero.

Integral and differential forms

For steady flow, mass flow in equals mass flow out: ∑m˙in​=∑m˙out​. For an incompressible fluid in a pipe,

Q=A1​V1​=A2​V2​,

with V the mean speed. Halve a pipe’s diameter and the speed quadruples.

Shrinking the control volume to a point with Gauss’s theorem gives

∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅(ρu)=0⇒∇⋅u=∂x∂u​+∂y∂v​+∂z∂w​=0

for incompressible flow. Any velocity field you invent must satisfy this to be physically possible, and CFD codes spend much of their effort enforcing it.

Worked exampleChecking fields and pipes

  1. On an 81 × 81 grid, the stagnation flow (x,−y) and the vortex (−y,x) have zero divergence (to 10−15) and zero net outflow through the boundary square.
  2. The expanding field (x,y) has divergence 2 everywhere and net outflow 8.0000 through the 2 × 2 square, equal to divergence × area, as Gauss requires. It can’t be an incompressible flow.
  3. A water main carrying 70 L/s: 0.990 m/s in the 300 mm section, 3.961 m/s in the 150 mm throat, 2.228 m/s in the 200 mm section, 70.0 L/s through each.

Exercise 1The thumb on the hose

A 16 mm garden hose delivers 0.3 L/s. A nozzle narrows the outlet to 5 mm. Find the speed in the hose and at the nozzle.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Hose area π⋅0.0162/4=2.011×10−4 m², so V1​=0.0003/2.011×10−4=1.492 m/s.
  2. Nozzle: V2​=V1​(16/5)2=1.492⋅10.24=15.28 m/s, fast enough to reach several metres. In reality the pump or mains pressure may not keep the flow rate constant when you restrict the outlet; that needs the energy equation (next lesson).

11.07.title: Bernoulli's equation
11.07.html:
Bernoulli’s equation is the most used and most misused result in fluid mechanics. It explains why a venturi meter measures flow, why a garden sprayer sucks up fertiliser, and why the pressure drops where a river speeds up between bridge piers. It also gets quoted for things it doesn’t explain. To use it properly, derive it and keep the assumptions in view.

Derivation along a streamline

Apply Newton’s second law to a fluid particle moving along a streamline, with coordinate s. Ignoring viscosity, the only forces are pressure and gravity:

ρ(∂t∂V​+V∂s∂V​)=−∂s∂p​−ρg∂s∂z​.

For steady, incompressible flow, V∂V/∂s=∂(V2/2)/∂s, and integrating along the streamline gives

p+21​ρV2+ρgz=constant along a streamline.

The terms are static pressure, dynamic pressure and hydrostatic pressure. Divided by ρg they become heads in metres.

When it lies

The assumptions: steady, incompressible (Mach number below about 0.3), inviscid (no friction losses), and along one streamline. The constant can differ between streamlines unless the flow is also irrotational. It fails across pumps or turbines (they add or remove energy), in long pipes (friction), in separated wakes, and through hydraulic jumps. The popular “equal transit time” explanation of wing lift is not Bernoulli; it’s just wrong.

The venturi meter

Combining Bernoulli with continuity, V1​A1​=V2​A2​, between an inlet of diameter D and a throat of diameter d gives

Q=Cd​A2​ρ(1−β4)2Δp​​,β=Dd​.

The discharge coefficient Cd​≈0.98 absorbs the small friction losses.

Worked exampleA 100/50 mm venturi

  1. A mercury manometer under water reads 150 mm, so Δp=(13546−998)⋅9.81⋅0.150=18.464 kPa.
  2. Throat area A2​=1.9635×10−3 m² and β4=0.0625, so the ideal throat speed is 2⋅18464/(998⋅0.9375)​=6.282 m/s and Q=0.98⋅A2​⋅6.282=12.089 L/s (ideal 12.336).
  3. Integrating the 1D Euler equation ρudu/dx=−dp/dx along a smooth contraction carrying the ideal flow gives a pressure drop of 18.4644 kPa: the same as Bernoulli and the manometer.
  4. Speed rises from 1.571 m/s at the inlet to 6.282 m/s in the throat.

Exercise 1What will the manometer read?

The same venturi will carry 10 L/s of water. What mercury manometer reading should you expect (ideal flow)?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V1​=0.01/(π⋅0.12/4)=1.273 m/s; V2​=4V1​=5.093 m/s.
  2. Δp=21​⋅998⋅(5.0932−1.2732)=12.134 kPa.
  3. h=12134/((13546−998)⋅9.81)=98.6 mm of mercury.

11.08.title: Torricelli and draining tanks
11.08.html:
How long does a rain-water tank take to empty through its tap? When will a leaking reservoir drop to half? In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli found that water leaves a hole at the speed a stone would reach falling from the free surface. Combined with conservation of mass, that gives a differential equation for the level, and a result that surprises most people: the second half of the water takes much longer than the first.

Torricelli’s law

Apply Bernoulli from the free surface (pressure atmospheric, speed nearly zero, height h above the hole) to the jet (atmospheric, speed V, height 0):

V=2gh​.

Real jets contract just outside a sharp-edged hole (the vena contracta) and lose a little to friction. The discharge coefficient Cd​≈0.61 for a sharp orifice accounts for both, so Q=Cd​a2gh​.

The draining equation

If the level falls slowly, the flow is quasi-steady: at each instant Torricelli holds with the current h. Mass conservation for a tank of cross-section A(h):

A(h)dtdh​=−Cd​a2gh​.

For a constant-area tank, separating variables gives h​=h0​​−2ACd​a​2g​t, and the time to empty is

tempty​=Cd​aA​g2h0​​​.

Because the outflow slows as h​, the bottom half of a cylinder takes 2​+1≈2.4 times as long as the top half. For other shapes, integrate numerically.

Worked exampleA rain-water tank

1.2 m diameter, 1.5 m of water, 25 mm sharp-edged outlet, Cd​=0.61.

  1. Initial outflow speed 2⋅9.81⋅1.5​=5.425 m/s; flow 1.624 L/s.
  2. Time to empty: 2088.7 s (34.81 min) from the closed form; RK4 gives 2088.7 s.
  3. The top half drains in 611.8 s, the bottom half in 1476.9 s.
  4. An inverted cone of the same top and height holds a third as much water and empties in 417.8 s by RK4 (exact 417.7), 0.20 of the cylinder’s time.

Exercise 1A bigger tap

Replace the 25 mm outlet with a 50 mm one. How long does the full tank take to empty, and how long to fall from 1.5 m to 0.5 m?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The hole area quadruples, so the time falls by 4: 34.81/4=8.70 min.
  2. From 1.5 to 0.5 m: t=Cd​aA​2g​2​(1.5​−0.5​)=3.68 min. Two thirds of the water leaves in 42 % of the total time.

11.09.title: The momentum theorem
11.09.html:
A fire hose bucks in your hands; a pipe bend in a hydropower plant needs a concrete anchor block weighing tonnes; a jet of water knocks a plate backwards. You don’t need to know the details of the flow inside to get those forces. Draw a control volume around the device and count the momentum going in and out.

The control-volume momentum balance

Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to momentum: the sum of forces on the fluid in a fixed control volume equals the rate of change of momentum inside plus the net momentum outflow. For steady flow with uniform inlets and outlets,

∑F=out∑​m˙V−in∑​m˙V.

The forces include pressure on the inlet and outlet faces (pA, pushing inwards), the force from the walls, and gravity. It’s a vector equation, so work component by component, and draw the control volume first.

Jets on vanes

A free jet is at atmospheric pressure everywhere, so only the vane pushes on it. A jet of mass flow m˙ and speed V turned by an angle θ pushes the vane with

Fx​=m˙V(1−cosθ).

A flat plate (θ=90°) feels m˙V; turning the jet right back (180°) doubles it.

Pipe bends

In a pipe the pressure terms usually dominate. For a horizontal bend turning the flow by θ, the force the fluid puts on the bend (and the anchor must resist) is

F=(p1​A1​+m˙V1​)e1​−(p2​A2​+m˙V2​)e2​,

where e1​ and e2​ are the inlet and outlet flow directions.

Worked exampleJets and a bend

  1. Water jet, 30 mm at 20 m/s: m˙=14.109 kg/s. Force on a vane turning it 90°: 282.2 N; 135°: 481.7 N; 180°: 564.4 N, exactly 2m˙V.

11.10.title: Angular momentum and turbines
11.10.html:
High in the Valais, water falls almost two kilometres through steel penstocks and leaves a nozzle at nearly 190 m/s, faster than a racing car. It hits the spoon-shaped buckets of a Pelton wheel, which turn it almost right round and send it dropping gently into the tailrace. How fast should the buckets move to grab the most energy? The angular momentum version of the control-volume balance answers that, and the same equation designs every pump, fan and turbine.

Euler’s turbomachinery equation

Apply the moment of momentum to a control volume around a rotor. In steady flow, the torque the fluid exerts on the rotor equals the angular momentum it loses:

T=m˙(r1​cu1​−r2​cu2​),

where cu​ is the tangential (swirl) component of the absolute velocity at inlet 1 and outlet 2. Power is P=Tω, and with blade speed u=ωr,

P=m˙(u1​cu1​−u2​cu2​).

It’s pure kinematics and momentum: no assumptions about viscosity or the flow inside the blade passage.

The Pelton wheel

For a Pelton, r1​=r2​ and u1​=u2​=u. The jet arrives at cu1​=V. Relative to the bucket it enters at V−u, is turned through an angle β (about 165°, so the water clears the next bucket), and leaves with absolute swirl cu2​=u−(V−u)cos(180°−β). Then

P=m˙u(V−u)(1+cos(180°−β)),

a parabola in u with its maximum at u=V/2. With a 180° bucket at u=V/2 the water leaves with zero absolute speed: all its kinetic energy goes to the runner. Real Peltons reach 90–92 %.

Worked exampleAn 800 m Pelton plant

Assumed: 800 m net head, 2 m³/s, nozzle velocity coefficient 0.98, 165° buckets.

  1. Jet speed 0.982⋅9.81⋅800​=122.78 m/s; hydraulic power ρgQH=15.70 MW.
  2. Sweeping the bucket speed, the best is 61.39 m/s =0.500V, giving 14.818 MW, an efficiency of 0.9440 before bucket friction, windage and bearings.
  3. An ideal 180° bucket at V/2 captures exactly the jet’s kinetic power, 15.074 MW.
  4. As a torque: a runner with 2.4 m pitch diameter turns at 489 rpm with 289.6 kN m, the same 14.818 MW.

A Pelton runner under 1883 m of head (an extreme Alpine scheme) drives a generator synchronised to 50 Hz at 428.6 rpm. With Cv​=0.98, what jet speed results, and what pitch diameter puts the buckets at half the jet speed?

  2. Best bucket speed u=94.18 m/s.
  3. D=60u/(πn)=60⋅94.18/(π⋅428.6)=4.20 m. At this head, speed rather than size limits the runner: the buckets see enormous centrifugal and impact loads.

11.11.title: Dimensional analysis in fluids
11.11.html:
The drag on a sphere depends on its diameter, its speed, and the fluid’s density and viscosity: five variables. Measuring every combination would take thousands of experiments. Dimensional analysis shows that only two dimensionless groups matter, so one curve describes every sphere in every fluid, from a sand grain settling in the Limmat to a weather balloon.

Buckingham’s Pi theorem

If a physical relation involves n variables built from k independent dimensions (mass, length, time), it can be rewritten as a relation between n−k dimensionless groups Π1​,…,Πn−k​.

The recipe:

  1. List the variables and their dimensions.
  2. Choose k repeating variables that between them contain all the dimensions but can’t form a group on their own (typically ρ, V, L).
  3. Combine each remaining variable with powers of the repeating ones so that all exponents of M, L and T vanish.

Finding the exponents is solving a linear system: each group is a vector in the null space of the dimension matrix. That’s what the code does, with exact fractions.

The famous groups

Group Definition Ratio
Reynolds Re=ρVL/μ inertia / viscous forces
Froude Fr=V/gL​ inertia / gravity
Mach Ma=V/c flow speed / speed of sound
Weber We=ρV2L/σ inertia / surface tension
Euler (pressure coefficient) Δp/(ρV2) pressure / inertia

For drag on a sphere, F, ρ, V, D and μ give F/(ρV2D2)=ϕ(Re). Engineers write it as the drag coefficient CD​=F/(21​ρV2A).

Worked exampleThe groups by computer

  1. Drag with repeating variables ρ, V, D: the null space gives Fρ−1V−2D−2 and μρ−1V−1D−1=1/Re, the textbook pair.
  2. A general flow with Δp, μ, g, σ, c, ρ, V, L (8 variables, 3 dimensions) gives 5 groups: Δp/(ρV2), 1/Re, gL/V2=1/Fr2, σ/(ρV2L)=1/We and c/V=1/Ma. The code checks each one is dimensionless.

Exercise 1Pressure drop in a pipe

The pressure drop Δp in a straight pipe depends on ρ, V, D, μ, the length L and the wall roughness ε. How many groups are there, and what are they?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. n=7 variables, k=3 dimensions, so 4 groups.
  2. With ρ, V, D repeating: Δp/(ρV2), Re=ρVD/μ, L/D and ε/D.
  3. Experiments show Δp is proportional to L, so Δp/(ρV2)=21​f(Re,ε/D)L/D: the Darcy-Weisbach equation, whose friction factor f fills the Moody chart (lesson 12.10).

11.12.title: Similarity and model testing
11.12.html:
Before a Swiss dam gets a new spillway, engineers build it at 1:30 or 1:50 in a laboratory hall, such as the VAW at ETH Zurich, and run water over it. A model is only useful if it behaves like the real thing, and that requires the right dimensionless groups to match. For open-water flows that’s the Froude number. It’s also why you can’t make every group match at once.

Similarity

A model is geometrically similar if every length scales by the same ratio λ=Lp​/Lm​. It’s dynamically similar if the ratios of all forces match, which means the relevant dimensionless groups are equal in model and prototype.

Froude scaling

Spillways, waves, ships and river works are dominated by gravity and inertia. Matching Fr=V/gL​ with the same g:

Vm​Vp​​=λ1/2.

Everything else follows from the dimensions:

Quantity Prototype/model ratio
Length λ
Velocity, time λ1/2
Discharge λ5/2
Force (same fluid) λ3
Pressure λ
Power λ7/2

The Reynolds problem

With water in both, the Reynolds number is λ3/2 times smaller in the model. Matching both Fr and Re would need a model fluid with viscosity λ3/2 times lower than water, which doesn’t exist. So modellers keep the model Reynolds number high enough (fully turbulent) that friction behaves similarly, and correct for the remaining scale effects.

Worked exampleA 1:50 spillway model

  1. Scale factors: velocity and time 7.07, discharge 17 677.67, force 125 000, power 883 883.
  2. A prototype discharge of 1500 m³/s becomes 84.85 L/s in the model; 8 m/s becomes 1.1314 m/s; a 30 s surge lasts 4.243 s.
  3. The Froude number is 0.8077 in both, while the Reynolds number drops from 8.0×107 to 2.26×105, a ratio of 353.6 =501.5.
  4. Matching Re too would need ν=2.83×10−9 m²/s.

Exercise 1Wave forces

In a 1:50 model of a harbour wall, waves with a 1.2 s period push on a wall section with a peak force of 12 N. What are the prototype wave period and force?

  1. Time scales with λ1/2=7.071: the prototype period is 1.2⋅7.071=8.49 s.
  2. Force scales with λ3=125000: 12⋅125000=1.5 MN. Seawater is about 2.5 % denser than the lab’s fresh water, so the real force is about 1.54 MN.

11.13.title: The Navier-Stokes equations
11.13.html:
Every flow in this course, the Limmat, the air over a cyclist, oil in a bearing, obeys one set of equations, written down by Navier in 1822 and Stokes in 1845. They’re Newton’s second law for a fluid parcel with the viscous stresses spelled out. Simple to write and famously hard to solve (proving that smooth solutions always exist in 3D is one of the Millennium Prize problems), they still have a handful of exact solutions that anchor everything else.

From Cauchy to Navier-Stokes

Newton’s law per unit volume for a fluid parcel is the Cauchy momentum equation:

ρDtDu​=∇⋅σ+ρg,

where σ is the stress tensor. For a Newtonian fluid it’s pressure plus viscous stress proportional to the strain rate: σij​=−pδij​+μ(∂ui​/∂xj​+∂uj​/∂xi​), the 3D version of τ=μdu/dy. Substituting, and using ∇⋅u=0 for incompressible flow:

ρ(∂t∂u​+(u⋅∇)u)=−∇p+μ∇2u+ρg,∇⋅u=0.

Four equations (three momentum components and continuity) for four unknowns (u, v, w, p).

Reading the terms

  • Unsteady ρ∂u/∂t: local acceleration.
  • Convective ρ(u⋅∇)u: nonlinear; the source of turbulence.
  • Pressure gradient −∇p: in incompressible flow, pressure is whatever it needs to be to keep ∇⋅u=0.
  • Viscous μ∇2u: diffusion of momentum.

Exact solutions

When the geometry makes the convective term vanish, the equations become linear and solvable. Between parallel plates with a pressure gradient dp/dx=−G, the flow is u=2μG​(h2−y2): plane Poiseuille flow. A rare unsteady solution with full nonlinearity is the Taylor-Green vortex, whose decay rate is set entirely by viscosity.

Worked exampleSymbolic verification

SymPy substitutes each field into continuity and both momentum equations and simplifies.

  1. Plane Poiseuille, u=2μG​(h2−y2), v=0, p=−Gx: residuals [0, 0, 0].
  2. Taylor-Green, u=Usinxcosye−2νt, v=−Ucosxsinye−2νt, p=4ρU2​(cos2x+cos2y)e−4νt: residuals [0, 0, 0].
  3. The same velocity with p=0 leaves 21​ρU2e−4μt/ρsin2x in the x-momentum equation: not a solution.
  4. Plane Poiseuille carries 2Gh3/(3μ) per unit width; mean/max = 2/3.

Exercise 1A narrow channel

Water (μ=1.0×10−3 Pa s) flows between two plates 2 mm apart under a pressure gradient of 1000 Pa/m. Find the flow per metre width and the centre speed, and confirm by substitution that Couette flow u=Uy/h, v=0, p constant also solves the equations.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Half-gap h=1 mm. q=2Gh3/(3μ)=2⋅1000⋅10−9/(3×10−3)=6.667×10−4 m²/s, about 0.67 L/s per metre.
  2. Centre speed Gh2/(2μ)=1000⋅10−6/0.002=0.5 m/s; mean =32​⋅0.5=0.333 m/s.
  3. Couette: ∂u/∂t=0; (u⋅∇)u=u∂u/∂x=0 since u depends only on y; ∇p=0; ∇2u=∂2(Uy/h)/∂y2=0. Every term vanishes, and ∂u/∂x+∂v/∂y=0.

11.14.title: Laminar pipe flow
11.14.html:
Olive oil running through a narrow pipe, blood in small arteries, water in a drip-irrigation line in a Bali rice field: when the flow is slow, narrow or viscous enough, it moves in orderly concentric layers. Then Navier-Stokes has an exact solution, found experimentally by Hagen in 1839 and Poiseuille in 1840. Its most striking feature: the flow rate goes with the fourth power of the radius.

The profile

Steady, fully developed flow in a round pipe has only an axial velocity u(r). Navier-Stokes in cylindrical coordinates reduces to

rμ​drd​(rdrdu​)=dxdp​,

with u(R)=0 at the wall and a finite value on the axis. Integrating twice:

u(r)=4μ−dp/dx​(R2−r2),

a paraboloid. Integrating over the cross-section gives the Hagen-Poiseuille law

Q=8μLπR4Δp​,uˉ=2umax​​.

Halve the radius and, at the same pressure drop, the flow falls to 1/16. That’s why narrowing arteries are so dangerous, and why viscometers use thin capillaries.

When it applies

Only for laminar flow, Re=ρuˉD/μ≲2300, and only once the profile has developed, after an entrance length of roughly 0.06ReD. Above that Reynolds number, disturbances grow and the flow becomes turbulent, with a flatter profile and far larger losses (lesson 12.10). A force balance on a cylinder of fluid also gives the wall shear stress, τw​=RΔp/(2L).

Worked exampleOlive oil in a 20 mm pipe

μ=0.084 Pa s, ρ=910 kg/m³, 5 m long, 2 kPa pressure difference.

  1. Q=π⋅0.014⋅2000/(8⋅0.084⋅5)=18.70 mL/s.
  2. Centre speed 0.1190 m/s, mean 0.0595 m/s: ratio 0.5000.
  3. Re=12.9, comfortably laminar.
  4. Wall shear stress 0.01⋅2000/(2⋅5)=2.000 Pa.
  5. A finite-volume solution of the radial equation reproduces the profile to 10−6 of the centre speed, and gives the same 18.70 mL/s.

Water (μ=1.0×10−3 Pa s) is pushed at 1 mL/s through a needle of 0.6 mm inner diameter and 25 mm length. Find the pressure needed across the needle, the mean speed and the Reynolds number.

  1. Δp=8μLQ/(πR4)=8⋅10−3⋅0.025⋅10−6/(π⋅(0.3×10−3)4)=7860 Pa, about 0.08 bar.
  2. Mean speed Q/(πR2)=3.537 m/s.
  3. Re=3.537⋅0.0006/10−6=2122: still just laminar. Push faster and the formula stops applying.

11.15.title: Vorticity and circulation
11.15.html:
Behind a boulder in a Bali river, a coconut can circle in an eddy for minutes before it escapes. You can explore that in the coconut lab. To describe such swirling flows, fluid mechanics uses two related quantities: vorticity, the local spin of each fluid parcel, and circulation, the total swirl around a loop. A surprise: in most of an eddy the water goes round without spinning at all.

Vorticity

Vorticity is the curl of the velocity,

ω=∇×u,ωz​=∂x∂v​−∂y∂u​ in 2D.

It equals twice the local angular velocity of a fluid parcel. A tiny paddle wheel carried by the flow would spin at ω/2. Flows with ω=0 everywhere are irrotational, and the next lesson builds them from potentials.

Circulation and Kelvin’s theorem

Circulation is the line integral of velocity around a closed curve:

Γ=∮u⋅dl=∬ωz​dA

by Stokes' theorem: the total vorticity inside. Kelvin’s circulation theorem says that in an inviscid, barotropic fluid with conservative body forces, the circulation around a loop moving with the fluid stays constant. Vorticity can’t be created inside such a flow; it comes from walls and is spread by viscosity. That’s why eddies are shed from boulders, bridge piers and wing tips.

The Rankine vortex

A simple model of an eddy: inside a core of radius a the fluid rotates like a solid body, uθ​=Ωr; outside it’s a free vortex, uθ​=Γ/(2πr). The core carries uniform vorticity 2Ω; outside, the vorticity is zero, so parcels orbit without spinning about their own axes. The circulation is Γ for every loop enclosing the core.

Worked exampleAn eddy behind a boulder

Γ=2 m²/s, core radius 0.4 m.

  1. Core angular velocity Ω=Γ/(2πa2)=1.9894 rad/s.
  2. Finite-difference vorticity on a 241 × 241 grid: 3.9789 in the core =2Ω; outside, zero up to a truncation error of 10−3.
  3. Circulation by line integral: 0.50000 m²/s around r = 0.2 m (vorticity × area), and 2.00000 around r = 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 m.
  4. Peak swirl 0.7958 m/s at the core edge. A coconut at r = 1 m circles once every 19.7 s.

Exercise 1Inside and outside the core

For the same eddy, how long does a coconut take to circle at r = 0.2 m and at r = 0.3 m? What’s the vorticity there, and the circulation around a 0.3 m loop?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Both radii are inside the core, where the fluid turns like a solid body: the period is 2π/Ω=2π/1.9894=3.158 s for both.
  2. Vorticity 2Ω=3.979 s⁻¹ at both.
  3. Circulation around r = 0.3 m: 2Ω⋅π⋅0.32=1.125 m²/s, less than the full 2 m²/s because the loop encloses only part of the core.

11.16.title: Potential flow and lift
11.16.html:
Away from walls and wakes, many flows are almost free of vorticity. For an irrotational, incompressible flow the velocity is the gradient of a potential, and the whole flow field can be built by adding simple pieces together. The method is old, but it still gives the most important result in aerodynamics: lift is proportional to circulation.

The velocity potential and stream function

If ∇×u=0, then u=∇ϕ. Continuity, ∇⋅u=0, turns this into Laplace’s equation,

∇2ϕ=0.

Laplace’s equation is linear, so solutions add. In 2D there is also a stream function ψ with u=∂ψ/∂y, v=−∂ψ/∂x; lines of constant ψ are streamlines. Both combine into one complex potential w(z)=ϕ+iψ of z=x+iy, and the velocity comes from a single derivative:

dzdw​=u−iv.

Building blocks

Flow w(z)
Uniform stream Uz
Source of strength m 2πm​lnz
Doublet zμ​
Vortex, circulation Γ (anticlockwise) −2πiΓ​lnz

A uniform stream plus a doublet of strength Ua2 gives the flow past a cylinder of radius a; adding a vortex gives a cylinder with circulation:

w=U(z+za2​)−2πiΓ​lnz.

Pressure, d’Alembert and Kutta-Joukowski

On the surface the speed is uθ​=−2Usinθ+Γ/(2πa). Bernoulli gives the pressure coefficient Cp​=1−(uθ​/U)2: +1 at the stagnation points and −3 at the top and bottom without circulation. That distribution is symmetric front to back, so the drag is zero: d’Alembert’s paradox. Real flows have drag because the boundary layer separates, as Phase 12 shows.

Circulation breaks the top-bottom symmetry. Integrating the pressure gives the Kutta-Joukowski theorem, valid for any 2D body:

L′=ρUΓper unit span.

A clockwise circulation (negative in the anticlockwise convention) lifts the body upwards. A wing creates its circulation through its sharp trailing edge; a spinning ball or a rotor ship drags it round with its surface (the Magnus effect).

Worked exampleChecking Kutta-Joukowski by integration

Air at ρ = 1.2 kg/m³, U = 10 m/s, a cylinder of radius a = 0.5 m.

  1. Without circulation: Cp​=1.000 at the stagnation points and −3.000 at the top and bottom. Integrating around 20 000 surface points gives drag and lift both below 10−13 N/m.
  2. With Γ = −20 m²/s (clockwise): lift 240.0000 N/m =ρU∣Γ∣=1.2⋅10⋅20. Drag is still zero.
  3. The stagnation points sit where sinθ=Γ/(4πUa): at −18.56° and 198.56°.
  4. At ∣Γ∣=4πUa=62.832 m²/s they merge at the bottom; lift is 753.9822 N/m.

Exercise 1A rotor ship

A Flettner rotor 3 m in diameter spins in a 12 m/s wind (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³). Model it as a cylinder with circulation Γ=2πaus​, where the surface speed is us​=36 m/s. Find Γ, the force per metre of rotor height, and the force on a 20 m tall rotor. Where are the stagnation points?

  4. Γ/(4πUa)=339.29/(4π⋅12⋅1.5)=1.5>1: the stagnation point has left the surface and a ring of air circulates with the rotor.

11.17.title: Open-channel flow and critical depth
11.17.html:
Rivers, irrigation canals and storm drains have a free surface open to the air. The water level is no longer fixed by a pipe wall: it adjusts, and that gives open-channel flow a behaviour pipes don’t have. The same discharge can flow deep and slow or shallow and fast, and the switch between them happens at one special depth.

Specific energy

Measure energy per unit weight from the channel bed. For a rectangular channel carrying discharge q per metre of width at depth y, the mean velocity is V=q/y and the specific energy is

E=y+2gV2​=y+2gy2q2​.

For fixed q, E is large both when the flow is very deep (the first term) and when it is very shallow (the second). In between there is a minimum.

Critical depth and the Froude number

Setting dE/dy=1−q2/(gy3)=0 gives the critical depth

yc​=(gq2​)1/3,Emin​=23​yc​.

At that depth V2=gy, so the Froude number Fr=V/gy​ equals 1. gy​ is the speed of a small surface wave, so Fr compares the flow speed with the wave speed:

  • Subcritical, Fr < 1: deep and slow. Waves can travel upstream, so downstream conditions (a gate, a weir) control the level.
  • Supercritical, Fr > 1: shallow and fast, like water on a spillway. Disturbances are swept downstream.

Every energy above Emin​ has two alternate depths, one on each branch.

Worked exampleA canal over a bed hump

A canal 3 m wide carries 6 m³/s, so q=2 m²/s, at a depth of 1.5 m.

  1. Critical depth yc​=(22/9.81)1/3=0.7415 m. A numerical search over 280 001 depths finds the minimum of E at 0.7415 m, with Emin​=1.1123 m =1.5yc​ and Fr = 1.0000 there.
  2. At 1.5 m: V = 1.333 m/s, Fr = 0.3476 (subcritical), E = 1.5906 m.
  3. The alternate supercritical depth with the same energy is 0.4167 m, with V = 4.799 m/s and Fr = 2.3735.
  4. A smooth hump on the bed lowers the available specific energy by its height. The largest hump the flow can pass without backing up (choking) is 1.5906−1.1123=0.4783 m.

Exercise 1A rice-field drain

A drain 0.5 m wide carries 0.08 m³/s. Find the critical depth and minimum specific energy. The water flows 0.3 m deep: what are V, Fr and the regime?

11.18.title: Weirs and Subak irrigation
11.18.html:
For a thousand years Balinese farmers have shared water through the subak, a cooperative system of canals, tunnels and terraces run from water temples. Water from a river weir is divided among channels by notched timber or stone dividers (tektek), then flows from terrace to terrace down the hillside, each one spilling over a low notch into the next. You can play with a full model in the subak lab. The hydraulics behind it is the weir.

Weirs from critical flow

A broad-crested weir is a raised sill long enough that the flow over it becomes critical. With upstream head H above the crest (approach velocity neglected), the specific energy over the crest is H, so the depth there is yc​=32​H and q=gyc3​​. For crest width b:

Q=Cd​b(32​)3/2g​H3/2≈1.705Cd​bH3/2 (SI).

A sharp-crested weir is a thin plate. Integrating Torricelli’s 2gh​ over the depth of the nappe gives

Q=Cd​32​2g​bH3/2,Cd​≈0.62.

Either way the discharge grows as H3/2, so measuring the head is measuring the flow. That’s why weirs are used as flow meters, and why a subak divider with notches of set widths splits the flow in proportion to those widths: every notch sees the same head.

A cascade of terraces

Treat each terrace as a tank of area A holding water up to the notch crest, then spilling into the next:

Adtdhi​​=Qi−1​−Qi​,Qi​=k(hi​−hcrest​)3/2.

The first terrace fills, starts spilling, and the wave of water moves down the hill. At steady state every notch passes the full inflow, so every terrace holds the same head.

Worked exampleA notch and a cascade

  1. A broad-crested notch 0.3 m wide passes 1.45 L/s at 2 cm head, 5.72 at 5 cm, 16.17 at 10 cm and 45.75 at 20 cm. A log-log fit has slope 1.500000.
  2. A sharp-crested weir of the same width at 10 cm head passes 17.37 L/s.
  3. Five terraces of 400 m², each holding 5 cm before it spills, with 0.3 m notches and 10 L/s from the canal. The first starts spilling after 400⋅0.05/0.010=2000 s (0.57 h on a one-minute record); the others follow at 1.82, 3.17, 4.52 and 5.88 h.
  4. After 12 h every terrace holds 12.26 cm: 5 cm plus a steady head of 7.258 cm. The outflow is 9.999 L/s, back to the inflow.

Exercise 1Sharing water fairly

A tektek divides a canal carrying 60 L/s into two notches, 0.2 m and 0.4 m wide, both broad-crested (Cd​=1) at the same crest height. Find the head and each share.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Total width 0.6 m: H=(0.6⋅1.7050.060​)2/3. With 1.705=(2/3)3/29.81​=1.7049: H=(0.05866)2/3=0.1510 m.
  2. The same head acts on both notches, so the shares split by width: 20 L/s and 40 L/s.
  3. Width is what sets each farmer’s share, not the head. That’s what makes the divider fair.

11.19.title: Hydraulic jumps
11.19.html:
At the foot of a spillway, water arrives thin and very fast. A little further on, the river is deep and slow. The change isn’t gradual: the surface leaps up in a churning, foaming roller called a hydraulic jump. You can see one in a kitchen sink, where the thin fast sheet under the tap suddenly thickens into a ring. Engineers build stilling basins to make jumps on purpose, because a jump destroys energy that would otherwise scour the riverbed.

Momentum, not energy

Energy isn’t conserved across a jump: turbulence turns it into heat. Momentum is the conserved quantity. For a short horizontal stretch of rectangular channel, the only horizontal forces are the hydrostatic pressures on the two ends, so the momentum function per unit width,

M=2y2​+gyq2​,

has the same value before and after. Solving M(y1​)=M(y2​) for the downstream depth gives the Belanger equation:

y1​y2​​=21​(1+8Fr12​​−1).

y1​ and y2​ are conjugate depths. The jump always goes from supercritical (Fr1​>1) to subcritical.

The energy lost

The specific energy drops by

ΔE=E1​−E2​=4y1​y2​(y2​−y1​)3​>0.

This is positive only when y2​>y1​. A reverse “jump” from deep to shallow would have to create energy, so it never happens. The stronger the jump, the larger the share of energy destroyed: about 2% at Fr1​=1.5 and over 70% at Fr1​=10. Designers aim for 4.5<Fr1​<9, where the jump is steady and efficient.

Worked exampleA stilling basin

Water leaves a spillway apron 0.25 m deep with q=2 m²/s.

  1. V1​=8.000 m/s and Fr1​=8/9.81⋅0.25​=5.1084.
  2. Bisection on M(y)=M(y1​) gives y2​=1.68542 m, matching Belanger to 9 digits. Downstream, Fr2​=0.2918.
  3. E1​=3.5120 m and E2​=1.7572 m, so the jump destroys 1.7548 m of head, the same as (y2​−y1​)3/(4y1​y2​).
  4. That’s ρgqΔE=34.43 kW dissipated in every metre width of the basin.

Exercise 1A sluice gate

Water shoots under a sluice gate 0.1 m deep at 5 m/s. Find Fr1​, the conjugate depth, and the head lost in the jump.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Fr1​=5/9.81⋅0.1​=5.0482.
  2. y2​=0.1⋅(1+8⋅5.04822​−1)/2=0.6657 m.
  3. ΔE=(0.6657−0.1)3/(4⋅0.1⋅0.6657)=0.6798 m. Check with energies: q=0.5 m²/s, E1​=0.1+25/19.62=1.3742 m, E2​=0.6657+0.52/(19.62⋅0.66572)=0.6944 m, difference 0.680 m.

11.20.title: Water hammer
11.20.html:
Shut a tap fast and the pipes bang. In a hydropower penstock, the same effect can burst steel. Water is nearly incompressible, but not quite. When a valve stops a long moving column, the water next to the valve stops first and is squeezed, and a pressure wave runs back up the pipe at roughly the speed of sound. This is water hammer.

The Joukowsky jump

Stop a slice of water moving at Δv in the time a wave crosses it. Momentum gives the pressure rise

Δp=ρaΔv,ΔH=gaΔv​.

With a≈1000 m/s, stopping water moving at only 1 m/s raises the pressure by about 10 bar. The wave speed is lower than sound in open water (1483 m/s) because the pipe wall stretches:

a=1+EeKD​K/ρ​​,

with K the bulk modulus of water, D the diameter, e the wall thickness and E the wall’s Young’s modulus.

Closure time and the method of characteristics

The pressure wave reflects at the reservoir as a relief wave and returns after 2L/a. If the valve closes faster than that, the full Joukowsky rise appears. Slower closures are softer, because relief waves arrive while the valve is still moving. For a velocity ramped down linearly over tc​>2L/a, the peak rise is Michaud’s

ΔH≈gtc​2LV0​​.

To simulate the full transient, write the 1D continuity and momentum equations along the two characteristics dx/dt=±a. On them the PDEs become ordinary relations:

C±:HP​=HA/B​∓ga​(VP​−VA/B​)−friction.

March in time with Δt=Δx/a and apply boundary conditions: fixed head at the reservoir, and the orifice law V=τV0​H/H0​​ at a valve whose relative opening τ falls from 1 to 0.

Worked exampleA penstock valve

A 600 m penstock from a reservoir with 100 m of head carries water at 2 m/s. Take a=1000 m/s. (A 0.5 m steel pipe with a 10 mm wall gives 1191.4 m/s by the formula above.)

  1. Joukowsky: ΔH=1000⋅2/9.81=203.874 m, about 20 bar. Round trip 2L/a=1.20 s.
  2. Method of characteristics with 40 reaches, instant closure: peak head 303.874 m, a rise of exactly 203.874 m. It holds for 1.200 s, then the wave reverses and the head swings down to −103.874 m. A real pipe can’t go below vapour pressure, so the water column would separate and cavitate.
  3. Closures in 0.6 s and 1.2 s also give the full 203.87 m.
  4. A linear velocity ramp over 3, 6 and 12 s gives 81.55, 40.77 and 20.39 m: Michaud’s formula exactly. Closing the valve area linearly gives 56.06, 23.66 and 10.93 m, because most of the flow reduction happens near the end, when relief waves are already arriving.

Exercise 1A closing time limit

For the same penstock, the pipe is rated for a head rise of at most 30 m. Using Michaud, how slowly must the valve close? What happens if a worker slams it shut in 1 s?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. tc​≥2LV0​/(gΔH)=2⋅600⋅2/(9.81⋅30)=8.155 s.
  2. 1 s is less than 2L/a=1.2 s, so the full Joukowsky rise of 203.9 m appears: about seven times the rating.
  3. That’s why large valves have slow-closing actuators, and penstocks have surge tanks.
